activities.anchor: The reason tokens come first is the same reason a workshop marks out before cutting
activities.caption: sequence the token workflow
activities.name: dsysTokenOrder

config.prompt: From decision to pixel — put the marking-out in order:
items: Choose the base unit — a 4 px spacing step
Build the ladders — spacing 4, 8, 12, 16, 24, 32, 48, 64; type at a 1.25 ratio from 16 px
Name the tokens — atomic design decisions held as data
Reference them everywhere — no pixel value outside the scale needs to exist
Fix once at the token level — the correction propagates everywhere
config.why: Every later decision references the tokens, so an error at that level propagates everywhere — and, mercifully, so does a fix.

activities.caption: true or false — what a token actually is
activities.name: dsysTokenJudge

statements.s: A token's value is the most important part of it.
statements.why: The value is the smallest part — the token is a decision, encoded as data.

statements.s: A spacing ladder built on a 4 px base unit contains 48 px as a valid step.
statements.why: 4, 8, 12, 16, 24, 32, 48, 64 — every value on the ladder exists; none outside it needs to.

statements.s: Hardcoded pixel values are fine as long as the design looks right.
statements.why: Untokenised values mute both the error propagation and the fix — the two properties that make tokens worth having.

statements.s: A type scale is usually a ratio applied to the body size.
statements.why: 16 px at a ratio of 1.25 gives 16, 20, 25, 31, 39, 49 — every heading and caption sits somewhere on that ladder.

activities.caption: atom, molecule or organism? file each part
activities.name: dsysAtomicSort

config.prompt: The atomic hierarchy — file each part at its level:

items.label: a search bar with label, input and hint

config.why: Parts compose into parts, and each level is only responsible for its own correctness — real systems blur the hierarchy, but the point survives.

activities.anchor: becomes a bottleneck — the classic calcification failure
activities.caption: walk the governance decision
activities.name: dsysGovernBranch

config.root: A new platform team of nine engineers arrives and asks how to work with the system. Walk the maintainer's response.

start.text: How do you respond to the new team?

choices.label: Show them the economics — what a screen costs composed versus hand-rolled
choices.feedback: The economics that drive adoption are simple to state and hard to arrange: compliance has to serve the team.

choices.label: Send them the mandate memo
choices.feedback: Adoption beats completeness — and measured teams report an adoption S-curve, not a memo S-curve.

hatch.text: The team needs one exotic component the system does not offer.

choices.label: Bless a documented, time-boxed escape hatch — contributed back later
choices.feedback: Mature systems explicitly bless the hatch rather than pretend it does not exist — chasing the last 20% usually costs more than it saves.

choices.label: Refuse — the system must cover every need
choices.feedback: The fork happens anyway, minus the documentation — and forks are how systems die.

done.text: Economics, a legitimate hatch, contributions flowing back: the system treated like a product with users.

mandate.text: Compliance demanded but not convenient is the shadow system's birth certificate: local overrides, forks, divergence.

chase.text: Below roughly 10 engineers, the honest recommendation is a lightweight kit — matching system weight to production scale is part of the economics too.

config.why: The hard part of a design system is not design; it is adoption — a federated model trades some coherence for throughput, and the escape hatch is part of the design.

activities.anchor: this is the accessibility lesson's payoff at scale
activities.caption: call the WCAG AA contrast bar
activities.name: dsysContrastEst

config.prompt: Finishing checks performed once and inherited everywhere — what contrast ratio does WCAG AA require for body text?
config.why: 4.5:1 for body text, 3:1 for large text and UI components — one check in the system instead of forty on forty screens.
config.context: Touch targets get floors too: 44 × 44 px (Apple) or 24 × 24 px (WCAG 2.2 minimum).

activities.anchor: the component API is the argument
activities.caption: pair each production scale with its system weight
activities.name: dsysScaleMatch

config.prompt: Match system weight to production scale — pair them:

pairs.right: hand-rolled decisions; a system would be overhead

pairs.left: batch — a product line with several surfaces
pairs.right: a lightweight kit: tokens plus a dozen core components

pairs.left: continuous — a platform, many teams shipping daily
pairs.right: the full apparatus: semantic layers, contribution processes, tests, release trains
one production line; each brand a token override

config.why: The public systems — Material, HIG, Polaris, Carbon — encode this maturity, and each documents not just components but a philosophy.

activities.anchor: The library is the visible artefact
activities.caption: find the faulty line — what a system is
activities.name: dsysLibrarySpot

config.prompt: One of these claims about design systems is backwards — click it:
lines: The component library is what everyone sees first.
The system is the library plus tokens, rules, documentation, contribution process and governance.
Industry surveys find the top challenges are adoption, funding and staffing.
If the components are well-designed, the system will run itself.
A library nobody can find or trust is a folder of good intentions.
config.correction: The hard part is not design — it is adoption: the surveys' top challenges are people-and-process ones, not component design.
config.why: Documentation is the product: usage guidance that says when NOT to use a component, playgrounds, and a clear contribution path.

activities.anchor: The break-even arrives when the per-screen cost falls
activities.caption: call the year-one build cost
activities.name: dsysBuildEst

config.prompt: A team of 30 engineers and 6 designers ships 40 screens a quarter. Before a system pays anything back, the first year of token and component work costs roughly how much?
config.why: About 100 person-days — after which the per-screen cost falls to roughly 1 person-day and the system saves ~50 person-days every quarter.
config.context: Below roughly 10 engineers the build cost usually exceeds year-one savings — the lightweight kit is the honest recommendation.
